input: The vapour-compression unit in question serves an ice rink, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. Between these two temperatures, the Carnot coefficient of performance is 6.07, which represents the theoretical maximum that any refrigerator operating between the same reservoirs could achieve. In practice, the installed unit achieves 2.49, a figure that comes from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated. This difference illustrates the various irreversibilities that are inevitably present in real equipment, including losses in the compressor, in the expansion process, and in the heat exchangers themselves. It is also worth bearing in mind that, because the rink's load varies over the season, the full-load figure may not be representative of everyday operation, and overall efficiency in service could differ appreciably from the tested value. Figures of this kind are nevertheless useful, because they allow the machine's performance to be judged against the best that the temperature levels permit, rather than against an arbitrary standard. At the same time, the absence of part-load data means that any broader judgement about the unit's performance across a full season would go beyond what the available evidence can support, and such a judgement should be made only with that limitation clearly in mind.
